query: For high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability to develop and retain a protective oxide layer that provides oxidation resistance? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison that would reveal it, the observations expected relative to a baseline, the applicable boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The ability of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) to develop and retain a protective oxide layer at high temperature is governed by the selective oxidation of key reactive elements (such as Al and Cr). In the disordered, multicomponent matrix of the HEA, these elements preferentially oxidize to form a thin, dense, and adherent oxide (e.g., Al2O3 and/or Cr2O3) that limits further oxygen ingress and metal cation diffusion.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous, polycrystalline HEA with a balanced concentration of reactive elements (e.g., Al and Cr) alongside other alloy components.
generation.intervention: Prepare two sets of HEA samples: one with standard (sufficient) levels of the reactive elements and another with systematically reduced levels of these elements.
generation.conditions: Expose the samples to a high-temperature, oxygen-rich environment (e.g., 800–1100°C in air) that simulates actual service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The highly disordered multicomponent matrix that slows down diffusion, thus promoting localized surface enrichment of reactive elements.
generation.mechanism: Selective oxidation of the reactive elements leads to formation of a continuous, self-limiting protective oxide layer. The sluggish diffusion in the HEA matrix limits both the inward diffusion of oxygen and outward migration of metal cations, stabilizing the protective scale.
generation.predicted_outcome: HEAs with sufficient reactive element content are expected to form a thinner, more continuous, and adherent protective oxide scale with lower overall oxidation (as measured by mass gain) compared to HEAs with reduced reactive element levels, which will form a more porous and less protective oxide layer.
generation.baseline: HEA samples with reduced concentrations of the reactive, oxide-forming elements that are anticipated to form non-protective, porous oxide scales and exhibit higher oxidation rates.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is anticipated to hold under high-temperature oxidation conditions (approximately 800–1100°C in oxygen-rich environments). Its validity outside this temperature range or under non-oxidizing atmospheres remains to be tested.
generation.uncertainty: While the overall qualitative behavior is supported by existing evidence, the precise quantitative differences in oxidation rate and oxide microstructure require further determination. Additionally, the influence of secondary alloying elements could modify the observed effects.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of otherwise identical HEA samples: one with the standard level of reactive elements (e.g., Al and Cr) and one with systematically reduced reactive element concentrations. Subject both sets to isothermal oxidation in air at a fixed temperature (within 800–1100°C) for an extended period sufficient to develop oxide scales. Characterize the oxide scales using microscopy, XRD, and gravimetric analysis.
measurements: Mass gain per unit area (via thermogravimetric analysis)
Oxide scale thickness and continuity (via microscopy)
Phase composition of the oxide scale (via X-ray diffraction)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA samples with reduced reactive element content develop oxide scales that are as continuous, dense, and protective, and exhibit oxidation kinetics (mass gain rates) similar to those of the standard samples, then the hypothesis—that selective oxidation of reactive elements supported by sluggish diffusion is the key mechanism for protective oxide scale formation—would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In alloys for high-temperature applications, at least one protective oxide among BeO, Cr2O3, Al2O3, and SiO2 are desirable to form, and that is why most of the alloys for high-temperature applications add these elements to form an oxide barrier for better oxidation resistance []. Previous studies have indicated that Cr2O3 is the sole stable phase in the Cr-O system, known for its compact structure and superior oxidation resistance []. However, it is noteworthy that Cr2O3 was not detected in the in situ XRD analysis conducted for this study. It can be reasonably inferred that non-existence of a Cr2O3 layer caused further outward diffusion of Mn, leading to the formation of Mn3O4, as can be seen from the XRD scan at a temperature of 950 °C.

cited_evidence.kind: web:3.2. High-Temperature Annealing in Air Environment
cited_evidence.text: The value of the Gibbs free energy of formation for ZrTiO4 is very low, indicating that it is a stable substance. Therefore, ZrTiO4 is continuously generated and polymerized along the periphery of TiO2 particles, and finally forms a dense oxide layer on the surface. The XRD pattern in Figure 7 shows that the ZrTiO4 phase appears and no other oxides are found after annealing at 800 °C for 1 h, indicating that the dense ZrTiO4 composite oxide layer formed on the surface effectively prevents the oxidation from continuing, which means that the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film still shows excellent oxidation resistance at 800 °C for 1 h in an air environment.

drafts.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys, the ability to develop and retain a protective oxide layer is governed by the selective oxidation of reactive alloying elements (such as Al and Cr) in a disordered, multi-element matrix. This selective oxidation forms a dense oxide (e.g., Al2O3 or Cr2O3) while the inherent sluggish diffusion kinetics of the HEA structure limit oxygen and metal transport, thereby preserving the scale’s integrity at high temperatures.
drafts.material_initial_state: A homogeneous, polycrystalline high-entropy alloy containing balanced proportions of reactive elements like Al and Cr.
drafts.intervention: Create a controlled comparison by preparing two sets of HEAs: one with standard (sufficient) concentrations of reactive elements and another with systematically reduced reactive element concentrations.
drafts.conditions: Exposed to high-temperature oxidation tests in an oxygen-rich atmosphere (e.g., at 900–1100°C) that simulate service conditions for high-temperature applications.
drafts.structural_mediator: The highly disordered multicomponent matrix of the HEA, which induces sluggish diffusion of both oxygen and metal species and enables localized enrichment of reactive elements at the surface.
drafts.mechanism: Selective oxidation leads to the formation of a dense, adherent protective oxide layer (like Al2O3 or Cr2O3) that inhibits further oxygen ingress. The slowed diffusion inherent to the HEA matrix further retards the transport of oxidizing species, reinforcing the protective nature of the scale.
drafts.predicted_outcome: HEAs with sufficient reactive elements will form a continuous, slow-growing, and adherent protective oxide layer with significantly lower oxidation rates compared to alloys with reduced reactive element content.
drafts.baseline: Conventional alloys or HEAs with lower reactive element levels that do not form a continuous protective oxide layer and thus experience higher oxidation rates under the same conditions.
drafts.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be valid for high-temperature conditions (around 900–1100°C) in oxygen-rich environments. Its relevance at lower temperatures or under different atmospheric conditions (e.g., corrosive gases other than oxygen) remains uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform high-temperature oxidation tests on two groups of HEAs: one with standard reactive element compositions and another with reduced reactive element amounts. Characterize the oxide scale using in-situ microscopy and gravimetric analysis to monitor oxide growth and continuity.
measurements: Weight gain due to oxidation over time
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEAs with reduced reactive element concentrations form oxide layers that are continuous, as protective, and exhibiting similar oxidation kinetics to those of the standard composition, the hypothesis—that selective oxidation aided by sluggish diffusion is the critical mechanism—would be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys, the innate multielement makeup leads to selective segregation of reactive alloying elements (such as Al, Cr, and/or Si) toward grain boundaries and defect sites during high-temperature exposure, which in turn nucleates and stabilizes a continuous, protective oxide layer.
drafts.material_initial_state: A homogeneous high-entropy alloy containing both reactive (e.g., Al, Cr, Si) and more inert elements, with no pre-existing elemental segregation.
drafts.intervention: Expose the alloy to a high-temperature oxidizing environment (with controlled oxygen partial pressure) that simulates service conditions.
drafts.conditions: Elevated temperatures where diffusion is activated yet below the threshold that destabilizes the protective oxide; typical oxidizing atmosphere with well-regulated oxygen content.
drafts.structural_mediator: Elemental segregation at microstructural features (grain boundaries or dislocation networks) that preferentially localizes reactive elements, thereby fostering oxide nucleation.
drafts.mechanism: During high-temperature exposure, reactive elements diffuse preferentially to grain boundaries or defect sites, leading to localized enrichment. This segregation promotes the formation of a dense, adherent oxide layer that acts as a barrier to further oxidation, thereby enhancing the oxidation resistance compared to a more uniformly composed alloy.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline HEA with a homogenously distributed reactive element content, the alloy with induced reactive element segregation will initially show more rapid localized oxide formation followed by a stabilization into a continuous, adherent protective layer. This manifests as lower overall oxidation rates (measured by weight gain and oxide thickness) and improved retention of mechanical properties during high-temperature exposure.
drafts.baseline: High-entropy alloy with a uniform distribution of reactive elements that does not promote early-stage formation of a continuous protective oxide, resulting in higher oxidation rates under similar conditions.
drafts.boundary: This mechanism is presumed effective under high-temperature conditions that activate elemental diffusion but remain within the stability regime of the protective oxides. It may not apply if processing conditions, alloy composition, or temperature regimes significantly alter segregation behavior or oxide stability.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples: one set that is thermally treated to enhance reactive element segregation (e.g., via controlled annealing) and another set maintaining a homogeneous distribution (using rapid solidification or short-term heat treatment). Expose both sets to identical high-temperature oxidizing conditions.
measurements: Weight gain over time as a measure of oxidation kinetics
Oxide layer thickness and morphology via microscopy techniques
Elemental mapping (e.g., using EDS) to verify segregation patterns
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both the experimentally segregated and homogeneous alloys display similar oxide layer characteristics, comparable oxidation rates, and no significant difference in performance, then the hypothesis that reactive element segregation is the key mechanism for developing the protective oxide layer would be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In high‐entropy alloys for high-temperature applications, the deliberate inclusion of slow‐diffusing elements such as Zr, together with reactive elements like Ti, drives the formation of a continuous, dense composite oxide (ZrTiO4) at the surface. This oxide layer acts as a robust barrier to both inward oxygen diffusion and outward cation migration, thereby enhancing oxidation resistance.
drafts.material_initial_state: An AlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy film with a homogeneous microstructure and well-mixed elemental distribution.
drafts.intervention: Prepare two alloy variants: one standard alloy (AlCrTiZrMo) and a comparative alloy with Zr removed (e.g., AlCrTiMo), while keeping all other processing and composition variables constant.
drafts.conditions: Exposure to air at an elevated temperature (e.g., 800 °C) for a fixed duration (e.g., 1 hour) to promote oxide scale formation.
drafts.structural_mediator: The formation and integrity of a dense, adherent ZrTiO4 composite oxide layer on the alloy surface.
drafts.mechanism: Zr, when alloyed with Ti, preferentially oxidizes to form ZrTiO4—a phase with low growth kinetics and high thermodynamic stability. This composite oxide effectively impedes oxygen ingress and cation egress by reducing diffusion rates at the interface, thereby limiting further oxidation of the underlying alloy.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The alloy containing Zr is expected to show lower mass gain, a thinner and more uniform oxide scale, and better oxidation resistance compared to the alloy lacking Zr, which should exhibit a higher mass gain and a more porous, less protective oxide layer.
drafts.baseline: An alloy variant (e.g., AlCrTiMo) that does not contain Zr and thus cannot form the ZrTiO4 phase, leading to a higher oxidation rate and a less protective oxide scale.
drafts.boundary: This mechanism is applicable under high-temperature oxidation conditions (around 800 °C in air) and during exposure times adequate for scale development (e.g., on the order of 1 hour); behavior in different atmospheres, longer exposures, or significantly different temperatures is not addressed by this hypothesis.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of HEA films with identical processing conditions: one with the composition AlCrTiZrMo (with Zr) and one with AlCrTiMo (without Zr). Subject them to high-temperature oxidation in an air environment at 800 °C for 1 hour. Characterize the oxide layers using in situ X-ray diffraction and cross-sectional scanning electron microscopy (SEM) with energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS), and measure the mass gain of each sample.
measurements: Oxide layer thickness and uniformity (via SEM)
Phase composition of the oxide layer (via XRD)
Elemental distribution across the oxide scale (via EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloy lacking Zr (AlCrTiMo) develops an oxide layer that is as continuous, dense, and protective—exhibiting similar mass gain and microstructural attributes—as the Zr-containing alloy, then the role of Zr in forming a protective ZrTiO4 composite oxide layer is not supported, thereby falsifying the hypothesis.

drafts.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys for high-temperature applications, the ability to develop and retain a protective oxide layer is controlled by the selective oxidation of minor elements (such as Al, Cr, and Si) that form dense, adherent oxides (e.g., Al2O3, Cr2O3, SiO2). When these elements are present in sufficient amounts, their slower cation diffusion relative to oxygen in-diffusion leads to the formation of a self-limiting, continuous oxide scale that acts as a barrier to further oxidation. In contrast, if these species are underrepresented, faster‐diffusing elements (such as Mn) form non‐protective oxides (e.g., Mn3O4) that cause depletion of the bulk and poor oxidation resistance.
drafts.material_initial_state: A well-homogenized high-entropy alloy with a baseline balanced composition that includes both protective-oxide-forming elements (Al, Cr, Si) and non-protective oxide formers (e.g., Mn) in their standard proportions.
drafts.intervention: Increase the relative content of protective-oxide-forming elements (e.g., add extra Al and/or Si) while keeping the overall alloy design constant.
drafts.conditions: Isothermal oxidation in air at high temperatures (800–1100 °C) for prolonged periods (e.g., 50 to 200 hours) to allow scale formation and steady-state oxidation kinetics to be observed.
drafts.structural_mediator: Formation of a continuous, adherent oxide scale whose thickness, density, and composition can be characterized by XRD and microscopy.
drafts.mechanism: The slower diffusion kinetics of key elements like Al, Cr, and Si compared to oxygen in-diffusion lead to the formation of a thin, self-limiting, protective oxide scale. This scale impedes further oxygen ingress and minimizes the outward diffusion of alloying elements, thereby preserving bulk composition and strengthening. In alloys deficient in these elements, faster diffusing species (such as Mn) oxidize to form non-protective, porous oxides, resulting in continued oxidation and degradation.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Alloys with an increased fraction of protective elements will display lower weight gain, the formation of a thinner and denser oxide scale (as evidenced by phase identification and microstructural analysis), and retention of bulk composition, compared to the baseline alloy which will show higher weight gain and the formation of non-protective oxide phases (e.g., Mn3O4).
drafts.baseline: The original HEA composition with standard levels of protective-oxide-forming elements, which under identical high-temperature exposure develops a thicker, less protective oxide scale including non-protective oxides.
drafts.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for high-temperature oxidation in air (800–1100 °C) and may not apply under reducing or non-oxidizing conditions or in alloys with radically different microstructures.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of otherwise identical HEA samples: one with the baseline composition and one with an increased concentration of protective-oxide-forming elements (e.g., extra Al and/or Si). Expose both sets to isothermal oxidation in air at a fixed temperature (e.g., 900 °C) for 100 hours.
measurements: Weight gain per unit area over time (via thermogravimetric analysis)
Phase identification of the surface oxides using in situ or ex situ X-ray diffraction
Microscopy to measure the thickness and density of the oxide layers
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the enhanced protective-element HEA does not exhibit a significantly lower weight gain rate, a thinner and denser continuously adherent oxide layer, or if it instead shows the same or worse oxidation behavior (e.g., formation of non-protective oxides) compared to the baseline alloy, then the hypothesis would be falsified.
